opus-5.5.text:
I think one of the most fundamental limitations of reinforcement learning, at least in the way it's typically practiced, is that it tends to learn a single monolithic policy that maps directly from observations to actions for one particular task. When you train that way, everything the agent knows gets baked into that one mapping. So if the environment changes a little, or you ask for a slightly different goal, or you combine two things it has seen separately, the policy often just doesn't generalize. You end up retraining from scratch, and that's extremely sample-inefficient.

Part of the reason is that the policy is essentially amortizing all the reasoning into a single feedforward pass. It doesn't have an explicit model of the world it can reason with at test time. Contrast that with how people operate: if I give you a new task you've never done before, you can think about it, simulate in your head what might happen, and compose bits of knowledge you already have to come up with a plan. That kind of test-time computation and compositionality is largely missing from standard model-free RL.

So a lot of my work has been asking: instead of learning a direct policy, can we learn models, for instance energy functions or generative models of the world, that capture constraints and dynamics, and then do planning or optimization over those at inference time? The nice thing is that these kinds of models can be composed. You can learn one model for one constraint and another for a different constraint, add them together, and get behavior that satisfies both, even if you never saw that combination during training. And you can spend more computation on harder problems by optimizing longer, rather than being stuck with whatever a fixed policy outputs.

There's also the reward specification issue. Designing reward functions that actually capture what you want is very hard, and RL agents are notoriously good at exploiting any loophole in the reward. Learning from data, like videos or demonstrations, and building generative world models from that, gives you a much richer signal than a single scalar reward.

So I wouldn't say RL is useless, it's clearly very powerful, especially for fine-tuning and in settings with good simulators. But I think for general-purpose intelligent agents, the limitation is this lack of generalization and compositionality that comes from learning one fixed policy, and I think we need approaches that bring in world models, planning, and reasoning at inference time to really get past that.

r001.rationale: The response says reward functions are hard to design to capture what people want and that agents exploit loopholes in them, conveying that RL does not ensure the agent learns the trainers’ intended behavior.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the core limitation of reinforcement learning, at least in the standard formulation, is that it's fundamentally built around optimizing a single reward signal. You define one objective, and the agent learns a policy that maximizes it. That sounds fine in a game like Go or Atari, where the reward is clean and the environment is fixed. But the real world doesn't work that way.

The problem shows up in a few places. First, specifying the reward is really hard. For almost any interesting task, the thing you actually care about is a messy combination of many considerations, and the moment you compress that into a scalar, you lose information. The agent then exploits whatever gaps exist between your proxy and your true intent. That's where you get reward hacking, and it's not a bug in the algorithm, it's a consequence of the framing.

Second, the policies you learn tend to be very brittle to the task you trained them on. If you train a policy to maximize reward A, and then tomorrow you want it to do task B, or task A under a new constraint, you basically have to retrain. The knowledge isn't composable. Humans don't work like that. We learn a lot of structure about how the world works, and then we can recombine that structure to pursive goals we've never seen before.

So the limitation, as I see it, is that RL ties together learning about the world and learning what to do in a way that's tightly coupled to one objective. That's why I've been more interested in approaches where you learn a model of the world, or learn energy-based or generative representations of what's possible, and then treat planning and decision making as a separate inference problem you can run on top. You can compose constraints, swap objectives, and generalize much better, because the heavy lifting was done learning structure rather than learning one specific behavior.

Sample efficiency is the thing people usually bring up, and it's real, but I think it's a symptom of this deeper issue. When all you have to learn from is a sparse reward signal, you're throwing away almost everything the environment is telling you.

r001.rationale: The response explains that an agent optimizes a scalar proxy and can exploit gaps between that proxy and the trainers’ true intent, identifying the lack of assurance that it learned what they intended.

astra-6.text:
I think one fundamental limitation is that reinforcement learning is driven by a reward signal, and that signal is often very sparse. It tells you whether you succeeded, but it doesn’t necessarily tell you much about how the world works or why an action failed. So you can end up needing an enormous amount of interaction to learn a particular task.

And once you’ve learned that task, the knowledge doesn’t automatically transfer to a different one. I think that points toward the importance of learning a more general model of the world—something you can use to reason about what might happen under different actions, rather than having to learn every behavior through trial and error.

r001.rationale: The response describes sparse rewards, high interaction costs, and weak transfer, but does not state that reinforcement learning lacks a guarantee of learning what its trainers intended.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one fundamental limitation is that reinforcement learning is typically tied to a particular reward function. You learn a policy to maximize that reward, but if you change the task, you often have to collect more experience and train again. That makes it difficult to reuse everything the agent has already learned about the world.

An alternative is to learn a model of how the world works—how it changes in response to your actions—and then use that model to plan toward different goals. The knowledge you acquire can then be useful across many tasks, rather than being encoded only in a policy for one objective.

r001.rationale: The candidate says reinforcement learning is tied to a particular reward and is hard to reuse across tasks. It does not identify the lack of a guarantee that the model learned what its trainers intended.
